---
title: Learning From Event Histories
description: Extend the payment model with transaction attributes, account context, and a merchant-repeat target.
---

The [transaction-history model](../tutorials/transaction-history.qmd) reads an
ordered sequence to predict a later dispute for each transaction. Now a payment
service also wants to anticipate repeat payments. Add the evidence that question needs:
how each payment was made and how long the account has been open. Then add a
second outcome to the same observation.

This is a richer transaction model, built after the basic training and
[evaluation workflow](evaluation.qmd). Keep the earlier model as a baseline
so you can test what each addition contributes.

## Keep Events And Account Context Together {#describe-the-evidence-before-the-architecture}

Consider a direct debit to an internet provider. Keep that latest payment once,
at the end of `trxns`, alongside the earlier transactions known at the decision
time. Repeated amounts and booking days supply evidence of a recurring pattern:

```yaml
account_age_days: 420
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-03-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    disputed: false
    repeats_next_30_days: true
  - booked_at: "2026-04-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    disputed: false
    repeats_next_30_days: true
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T08:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    channel: card
    disputed: true
    repeats_next_30_days: false
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    disputed: false
    repeats_next_30_days: true
```

The transaction list is the **event history**, including the payment being
scored. Each event keeps its amount, merchant, channel, and booking date
together. `account_age_days` supplies **profile context** shared by the sequence.
Use its value as known at the decision time.

| Evidence | What it contributes |
| --- | --- |
| Amount, merchant, and channel within one event | Distinguishes a direct debit from a card purchase, even at the same merchant. |
| Ordered transactions and booking dates | Exposes repeated amounts, merchant visits, and calendar patterns. |
| Account profile | Supplies context shared by the transaction sequence, such as account tenure. |

A calculated mean payment amount or dominant channel is another possible
input. Compare those summaries with the event sequence to learn whether
preserving individual transactions is useful.

Sort by booking time, oldest to newest. `DateParts` represents recurring
calendar patterns in the booking day, weekday, and hour. It does not encode
elapsed time between transactions. The sequence ends with the latest payment;
records after that decision are excluded.

The snapshot cutoff is the final booking time, May 28, 2026 at 09:00. For every
listed transaction, `disputed` records whether a new dispute against it was
reported in the 30 days after that cutoff. `repeats_next_30_days` records whether
another payment to that transaction's merchant occurred in the same future
window. All transaction predictions use the complete sequence known at this
common cutoff.

## Learn Two Outcomes From The Same History {#ideas-from-transaction-and-time-series-models}

Place both targets inside `trxns`, beside the transaction they describe.
`mask=True` hides each transaction's answers and supplies their supervision.
The two predictions share encoded context, with their own decoders and
supervision. This lets the application test a joint
model against separate models for the two decisions:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    account_age_days=rf.Number,
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        channel=rf.Enum(values=("card", "direct_debit", "bank_transfer")),
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
        repeats_next_30_days=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/context/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/context/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)
```

These application-supplied Parquet files keep profile context at the root and
all transaction fields inside `trxns`. Every listed transaction supplies both
Boolean labels. Their schema addresses are `/trxns/disputed` and
`/trxns/repeats_next_30_days`.

Prediction files omit both outcome fields from every transaction while keeping
the transaction records. Output format 2 returns results inside
`predictions.trxns`, with `inferred: true` for both targets at every retained
transaction position. See [Prediction Output](prediction-output.qmd).

Shared context lets you test whether learning the account's behavior helps
both tasks. Inspect each outcome separately: improvement on repeat payments
can accompany a regression in dispute detection. For repeat payments, measure
precision and recall for another payment to each transaction's merchant within
the common 30-day window.
For disputes, measure recall at the team's review capacity. A dispute label
records a later customer outcome and needs its own operational definition.

## Choose A Learning Workflow

With settled outcome labels, train the supervised model directly. When you
have many more histories than labels, first hide sampled transaction amounts
or merchants and learn to reconstruct them from the remaining context. That
gives unlabeled activity a learning role before adapting the model to dispute
or repeat-payment prediction.

Reconstructing a hidden transaction value asks what fits the observed
sequence. Predicting a later outcome asks what happens after the decision.
Define and evaluate those objectives separately. The
[pretraining guide](pretraining.qmd) shows how to change objectives while
reusing compatible learned state.

You can also export a **contextual representation**: learned vectors combining
the account fields and its history. Keep the encoder fixed while training
separate task predictors on those vectors. This tests whether the learned
context is useful for another outcome before updating the encoder for it.
[Embeddings](../core-concepts/embeddings.qmd) explains that workflow.

The next structural extension is [Transaction And Account Outcomes](../case-studies/customer-risk.qmd):
nest line items inside transactions, add a separate withdrawal history, and
combine transaction dispute targets with an account-level loss target.

## Make The Comparison About The Decision

For repeat payments, compare with rules based on merchant, amount, and the
booking calendar.
For disputes, compare with the existing tabular model and its history features.
Keep the eligible payments, available evidence, and outcome windows identical.

Test each addition in sequence: history versus the payment alone, channel and
profile versus history alone, then joint targets versus separate models.
Later, compare reconstruction pretraining with the same supervised model
trained from scratch. [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd) explains these comparisons.

## Forecast A Future Value

As an optional transfer to another event domain, a market-data application
can supply daily bars and ask for the next trading day's closing price. A bar
is a multivariate event: opening, high, low, and closing prices plus volume
belong to the same interval. The history-and-target pattern stays the same:

```python
market_model = rf.Model.xs(
    daily_bars=rf.Branch(
        length=64,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        open=rf.Number,
        high=rf.Number,
        low=rf.Number,
        close=rf.Number,
        volume=rf.Number,
    ),
    next_close=rf.Number(mask=True),
)
```

Each bar keeps its price and volume measurements together. Prepare observations
at the end of a trading day, including only completed bars known then.
`booked_at` supplies calendar context for each completed bar, not elapsed-time gaps. The
`next_close` label comes from the following trading day and becomes available
after that day closes. Train from Parquet files through `ArrowDataModule`, as
above, using files prepared for this market schema.

This defines one future-value prediction. If the application needs several
future steps, define their target structure and evaluation horizon explicitly.
Include a last-known-close baseline when evaluating this forecast.

[Business Prediction Examples](../case-studies/relational-tasks.qmd) applies
the approach to customer retention, reviewer engagement, and study reporting.
